articles.title: Deregulation, Not Data Centers, Broke the Grid
articles.author: Edgardo Sepulveda
articles.content_excerpt: The public attribution of blame for rising electricity costs is half right. Data centers are indeed driving the first sustained surge in American electricity demand in more than a generation. But the historical record shows that electricity demand — what the industry calls “load” — has grown this quickly before without pushing prices up. What is different this time is not the load itself but the fact that it is landing on deregulated electricity markets that were never built to absorb growth. Today, about a third of US retail electricity sales are in deregulated markets; the rest are served by traditional regulated utilities. articles.title: Ansar Allah’s Red Sea Advance Has Exposed Saudi Weakness
articles.author: Arron Reza Merat
articles.content_excerpt: On September 9, Yemen’s Ansar Allah, or “Houthis” as they are also known, descended from the highlands down roads and riverbeds to the Tihamah coastal plain and captured the port of Mokha from the Saudi-based government the following day. By September 11, they had taken Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Since then, they have used that position to blockade Israel and exercise leverage over the Saudi kingdom.Ansar Allah went on to shut down the 745-mile-long East–West pipeline that transports four to five million barrels per day from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil fields to its Red Sea export terminals, possibly with the assistance of Iraqi militias. articles.title: A Portrait of How Workers Build a Strike
articles.author: Luis Feliz Leon
articles.content_excerpt: I was at a Crotona Park barbecue in the South Bronx to celebrate my wife’s nephew, who was going off to a trade school after graduating high school. The family barbecue included a cross section of union members, among them electricians, hotel workers, Teamsters — not a strange amalgam, thanks to New York’s high union density . It’s often only in TV shows that you see a tight-knit group of friends from vastly different class backgrounds hanging out together. In real life, we can’t curate a social circle of people from disparate backgrounds with the same ease you assemble an eclectic wardrobe from a thrift store. articles.title: AI Doomsaying Is an Aggressive Sales Pitch
articles.author: Richard Seymour
articles.content_excerpt: It seems a strange publicity gambit for an industry to assert that its own product could wipe out humanity. In the lingo of our evolving tech empire, though, this is exactly what is meant by “criti-hype.” The term was coined by Lee Vinsel at Virginia Tech, who defined it as “criticism that both feeds and feeds on hype.” When Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic recently, he claimed that there is a high chance that AI could develop into a superintelligence that escapes human control, triggering a sequence that causes human extinction. Evan Hubinger, who remains with the company, backed him up , saying that Anthropic is trying to prevent this but hasn’t dealt with the problem yet. articles.title: Does Dollar Supremacy Help Americans?
articles.author: Dominik A. Leusder
articles.content_excerpt: It is scarcely possible to explain the convulsions of the twenty-first century without accounting for the pivotal role of the global dollar system. The financial crisis, the emergence of a new global monied elite, and the rise of China are inseparable from the dollar’s status as the world’s preeminent currency and the benefits and burdens it confers on different actors. articles.title: Elected Officials Are Facing a Reckoning Over Their Collusion with Big AI
articles.content_excerpt: A majority of Americans want to put a stop to the profit-driven artificial intelligence (AI) agenda being pushed onto all of us by a handful of powerful tech corporations. Across the country, people are building a movement to protect our water, our air, our children, our schools and our jobs from Big Tech. We are not afraid of AI or technology, we’re just not buying the version of AI these corporations are peddling. We come to this fight from different places and perspectives. Stephanie is fighting against the construction of a nuclear weapons data center in Michigan that will reshape her community. articles.title: The Jewish Socialists Who Fought the Tsar and Zionism
articles.author: Molly Crabapple
articles.content_excerpt: Jewish socialist intellectuals founded the Bund in the Russian Empire in 1897, and it soon became a mass organization of the Jewish working class — a working class confined by law to the Pale of Settlement. From its inception, the Bund and the socialist politics it represented struggled against capitalists and autocrats alongside non-Jewish socialist comrades. It also competed bitterly with its Jewish rivals: Orthodox traditionalists, Zionists, and Bolsheviks. Amid repression and revolution, the story of the Jews of the western Russian Empire diverges. Huge numbers emigrated to the Americas, and more than anywhere to New York City, where they built a Yiddish-speaking socialist world whose inheritors are in many ways today’s anti-Zionist socialist Jews. articles.title: M*A*S*H is an Antiwar Masterpiece
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content_excerpt: In December of last year, I started watching the television show M*A*S*H , which ran on CBS from 1972 to 1983. As a history nerd with a penchant for old TV shows I quickly became obsessed, watching every single episode in under six months. For those unfamiliar, the show is a comedy-drama following the exploits of the personnel serving at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital (M*A*S*H) during the Korean War (1950-1953). Intended as an allegory for the Vietnam War, the show tapped into the intense anti-war and anti-institutional sentiment of broad swaths of the American public of the time. The show is unapologetically anti-war and progressive, unrelenting in its insistence that basic human dignity be upheld in the most horrific circumstances. articles.title: The Call for Working-Class Liberalism Is Coming From Inside the House
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content_excerpt: The socialist left has a vexed relationship with major economists. This is a problem, because it sometimes leaves the Left on the outside of contemporary economic debates. Daron Acemoglu is precisely the sort of economist that the Left should not ignore. Alongside his frequent collaborators Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson, he is a 2024 Nobel laureate in economics. He is also among the world’s most cited economists. His new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , has already received lot of attention, as his recent spat with The Economist shows. Acemoglu’s work can be summed up in the proposition that institutions matter for economic growth. He identifies two types of institutions.
